claims.text: The starting material is an as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloy.
The as-deposited alloy has an ordered, single-phase hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited alloy undergoes a sharp, hysteretic, first-order magnetostructural transition.
Post-deposition annealing can introduce fine second-phase precipitates and thereby produce controlled nanoscale heterogeneity in this alloy.
Post-deposition annealing can reduce the grain size of the as-deposited alloy.
Annealing temperature and duration can calibrate the extent and length scale of the resulting heterogeneity.
Grain boundaries and nanoscale precipitates act as dispersed transformation fronts for the magnetostructural transition.
These transformation fronts lower local energy barriers for the magnetostructural transition.
Engineered nanoscale heterogeneity creates a distribution of local transition temperatures.
A distribution of local transition temperatures broadens the overall magnetostructural transformation.
Lower transformation barriers reduce the energy barriers responsible for magnetic or thermal hysteresis.
Broadening the transformation produces a smoother entropy-change profile.
A smoother entropy-change profile enhances heat exchange during magnetic cooling.
Optimally annealed samples will have a smaller hysteresis width than the as-deposited baseline under low-field cycling.
Optimally annealed samples will exhibit a broader transition-temperature interval than the as-deposited baseline.
Optimally annealed samples will exhibit faster heat exchange than the as-deposited baseline under low-field conditions.
The predicted improvements are restricted to an annealing window that creates nanoscale heterogeneity without extensive secondary-phase formation or loss of mechanical integrity.
The magnitude of hysteresis reduction and transition broadening depends sensitively on annealing parameters and the resulting microstructure.
Failure to obtain statistically significant transition broadening and hysteresis reduction despite confirmed microstructural heterogeneity would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
